justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift assumption from what appears to be a baseline around 368–370 for this asset. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, assuming minimal drift and mean-reverting intraday dynamics, which produced an estimate of 370.5. For the one-week horizon, I allowed for a slight positive drift of roughly 0.4%, consistent with a modest bullish bias but well within normal weekly variation. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 375 reflects compounding that same gentle drift over approximately four weeks, though I held the directional conviction loosely given how much can change over a month.

The confidence interval widths were primarily driven by realized volatility scaling. Daily volatility for an asset in this range is typically on the order of 0.5–1%, so the one-day interval of 360–381 reflects roughly ±1.5 standard deviations of expected daily movement. As the horizon extends, uncertainty compounds approximately with the square root of time, which is why the one-week interval (±20 points) and the one-month interval (±40 points) widen accordingly. I also factored in that autocorrelation and trend persistence tend to break down at longer horizons, adding some additional uncertainty beyond pure volatility scaling.

There are several risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise macro catalyst — such as a dovish central bank pivot, a strong earnings beat in a correlated sector, or a short-squeeze dynamic — could drive prices well above 381 even within a single day. On the downside, a risk-off episode triggered by geopolitical escalation, an inflation surprise, or a liquidity shock could push the asset below 360 quickly. At the monthly horizon, structural regime changes — a sustained shift in interest rate expectations or a broad equity market correction — represent the most plausible tail scenarios that my intervals do not fully capture.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume relatively stable market conditions and do not explicitly model jump risk or gap openings. In practice, binary events like central bank announcements, major economic data releases, or unexpected geopolitical developments can produce discontinuous price moves that fall entirely outside a normally distributed confidence band. These fat-tail risks are real and should be treated as genuine sources of additional uncertainty beyond what the stated 90% intervals convey.
